title: Four great vows
hookLine: beings are numberless, I vow to free them; delusions are endless, I vow to end them (as chanted in Zen)

cards: The last bell of the evening sit rings in a Zen hall. Nobody stands up yet. Instead, the whole room starts to chant together, in a low and even voice.
The first line goes something like this: beings are numberless; I vow to free them. The second: delusions are endless; I vow to end them. Then two more lines, and the room goes quiet.
Said slowly, it sounds calm. Heard closely, it sounds impossible. Numberless, and I vow.

teach.b: First, the four lines. English versions differ, and each community keeps its own, but the shape holds. Beings without number: I vow to free them.
Delusions without end: I vow to end them. Gates of the teaching beyond measure: I vow to enter them. The Buddha's way, with nothing above it: I vow to become it.
Each line names something too large, then makes a promise anyway. Second, why say something impossible. A vow you can finish is a task.

teach.h: A VOW YOU CAN'T FINISH IS A DIRECTION.
teach.b: A vow you can't finish is a direction, the way a compass points north without ever arriving there. The bodhisattva, earlier in this block, was one who seeks awakening for the sake of all beings.
These four lines are that wish, said out loud, often, with other people.
Third, why together, and again. In Zen and in other Mahayana communities, the vows are chanted at the end of a sit, at ceremonies, at the start of retreats. Said once, a vow is a decision.
Said every evening, it becomes a habit of the heart, worn smooth like a stair.
Fourth, where this week has been: Samantabhadra and his great vows, Maitreya, the one to come, Ksitigarbha in the lowest places, then skillful means, the perfection of wisdom and its mother.
Now the vows themselves, in four lines short enough to carry.
Numberless, I vow. The first word admits the size of the job. The next two start it anyway.

how: In Zen and other Mahayana communities the four great vows are chanted together, often at the end of a meditation period, at ceremonies and at the start of retreats, each community in its own version.

o: four rules a monk must keep to stay in the order

four vows, each too large to finish, made anyway

games.q: the vow says beings are numberless. you can't free them all. what does the chant do next?
o: shrink it to a number you can manage
games.why: numberless, and I vow. the size is admitted in the first word and the promise is made in the next.

practice: Take the four vows on four breaths, in your community's version if you chant them, or just letting the shapes pass through if you don't. On each out-breath: numberless; endless; beyond measure; nothing above it.
Then sit with whatever's left, the size of it, and the small steady breath that keeps going anyway.

wordCard.voice: Four great vows. Beings, delusions, gates of the teaching, the Buddha's way: each too large, each vowed anyway. Chanted in Zen halls after the sit. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a vow or resolve, the word for a bodhisattva's great vows.

carryVoice: Your line: numberless, I vow. Too big to finish, and begun anyway. That's the week.
